What happens if soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to you? They will not prove submissive, and unless submissive they will be practically useless.
What happens if punishments are not enforced after soldiers have become attached to you? They will still be useless.
How should soldiers be treated? With humanity in the first instance, but kept under control by means of iron discipline; this is a certain road to victory.
How is discipline affected by habitually enforced commands? If commands are habitually enforced in training, the army will be well-disciplined; if not, its discipline will be bad.
What is the gain when a general shows confidence in his men but insists on obedience? The gain will be mutual.
What are the six kinds of terrain? Accessible ground; entangling ground; temporizing ground; narrow passes; precipitous heights; and positions at a great distance from the enemy.

What is accessible ground and how should it be used? Ground which can be freely traversed by both sides; be before the enemy in occupying the raised and sunny spots, and carefully guard your line of supplies, then you can fight with advantage.

What is entangling ground and what are its risks? Ground which can be abandoned but is hard to re-occupy; if the enemy is unprepared you may sally forth and defeat him, but if he is prepared and you fail, return being impossible, disaster will ensue.

What is temporizing ground and how should it be used? Ground where neither side will gain by making the first move; even if the enemy offers an attractive bait, do not stir forth but retreat, enticing him in turn, then attack part of his army with advantage.

What is the rule for narrow passes? If you can occupy them first, garrison them strongly and await the enemy; if the enemy forestalls you, do not go after him if the pass is fully garrisoned, but only if it is weakly garrisoned.

What is the rule for precipitous heights? If you are beforehand, occupy the raised and sunny spots and wait for the enemy to come up; if the enemy has occupied them first, retreat and try to entice him away.
What is the rule when situated at a great distance from an equal enemy? It is not easy to provoke a battle, and fighting will be to your disadvantage.
What must a general in a responsible post carefully study? The six principles connected with Earth.

What are the six calamities an army is exposed to? Flight; insubordination; collapse; ruin; disorganization; and rout; these do not arise from natural causes but from faults for which the general is responsible.
What causes flight? Other conditions being equal, if one force is hurled against another ten times its size, the result will be the flight of the former.

What causes insubordination and collapse? When the common soldiers are too strong and their officers too weak, the result is insubordination; when the officers are too strong and the common soldiers too weak, the result is collapse.

What causes ruin? When the higher officers are angry and insubordinate, and give battle on their own account from resentment before the commander-in-chief can tell whether he is in a position to fight, the result is ruin.

What causes utter disorganization? When the general is weak and without authority, his orders not clear and distinct, no fixed duties assigned to officers and men, and the ranks formed in a slovenly haphazard manner, the result is utter disorganization.

What causes rout? When a general cannot estimate the enemy's strength, allows an inferior force to engage a larger one, or hurls a weak detachment against a powerful one, and neglects to place picked soldiers in the front rank, the result must be rout.
What must a general in a responsible post carefully note? The six ways of courting defeat.

What is the soldier's best ally, and what is the test of a great general? The natural formation of the country is the soldier's best ally; a power of estimating the adversary, of controlling the forces of victory, and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances constitutes the test of a great general.

What distinguishes the general who wins from the one who is defeated? He who knows these things and puts his knowledge into practice will win his battles; he who knows them not nor practices them will surely be defeated.

When must a general fight even against the ruler's bidding, and when must he not? If fighting is sure to result in victory he must fight even though the ruler forbid it; if fighting will not result in victory he must not fight even at the ruler's bidding.

Who is the jewel of the kingdom? The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign.
How should soldiers be regarded? As your children, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys; as your beloved sons, and they will stand by you even unto death.

What happens if a general is indulgent but cannot make his authority felt? If he is kind-hearted but cannot enforce commands, and incapable of quelling disorder, his soldiers are like spoilt children, useless for any practical purpose.
When have we gone only halfway towards victory regarding our own men? If we know our men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the enemy is not open to attack, we have gone only halfway.
When have we gone only halfway regarding the enemy? If we know the enemy is open to attack, but are unaware that our own men are not in a condition to attack, we have gone only halfway.

When have we still gone only halfway regarding the ground? If we know the enemy is open to attack and our men are in a condition to attack, but are unaware that the nature of the ground makes fighting impracticable, we have still gone only halfway.
What is true of the experienced soldier once in motion? He is never bewildered; once he has broken camp, he is never at a loss.
What makes victory complete? If you know the enemy and know yourself, your victory will not stand in doubt; if you know Heaven and know Earth, you may make your victory complete.
How does a ruler hobble his army? By commanding it to advance or retreat, being ignorant of the fact that it cannot obey.
How does governing an army like a kingdom cause trouble? It causes restlessness in the soldiers' minds, because the ruler is ignorant of the conditions which obtain in an army.
How does employing officers without discrimination shake confidence? It ignores the military principle of adaptation to circumstances, and thereby shakes the confidence of the soldiers.

What is the method of attacking by stratagem? To subdue the enemy's troops without fighting, capture their cities without siege, and overthrow their kingdom without lengthy operations, so that with forces intact one disputes the mastery of the Empire without losing a man.

What is the rule for unequal forces in battle? If ten to one, surround; if five to one, attack; if twice as numerous, divide; if equally matched, offer battle; if slightly inferior, avoid; if quite unequal, flee.
What is the significance of the general as bulwark? If the bulwark is complete at all points the State is strong; if defective, the State is weak.

What five conditions guarantee victory? Knowing when to fight and when not; handling superior and inferior forces; one spirit throughout the ranks; being prepared while the enemy is unprepared; and having military capacity without interference from the sovereign.

How does the good fighter secure himself and wait? He first puts himself beyond the possibility of defeat, then waits for the enemy's vulnerability; security lies in his own hands, opportunity in the enemy.
What does defensive versus offensive indicate? The defensive indicates insufficient strength; the offensive, superabundance of strength.
How does the expert in defense and attack act? The defender hides in the most secret recesses of the earth; the attacker flashes forth from the topmost heights of heaven.

Why are easy victories not praised? Because the clever fighter wins with ease, and his victories bring him neither reputation for wisdom nor credit for courage; he wins by making no mistakes, conquering an enemy already defeated.
What is the posture of the victorious strategist? He seeks battle only after the victory has been won; the one destined to defeat first fights and afterwards looks for victory.
How does the consummate leader control success? By cultivating the moral law and strictly adhering to method and discipline.
What are the five steps from measurement to victory? Measurement, estimation of quantity, calculation, balancing of chances, and victory, each arising from the one before.
How does a victorious army compare to a routed one? As a pound's weight against a single grain.
What is the onrush of a conquering force like? Pent-up waters bursting into a chasm a thousand fathoms deep.
How is a large force controlled? By dividing up its numbers, as with a few men.
What makes a large army fight like a small one? Signs and signals.
How is the host made to withstand attack unshaken, and its impact like a grindstone on an egg? By direct and indirect maneuvers, and by the science of weak points and strong.
How are direct and indirect methods used? The direct for joining battle, the indirect for securing victory; their combinations are inexhaustible.
How do the five notes, colors and tastes illustrate tactics? Their limited combinations yield endless melodies, hues and flavors, just as the direct and indirect yield endless maneuvers.
How do the direct and indirect relate? They lead on to each other in turn, like moving in a circle that never ends.
What are the onset of troops and the quality of decision like? The onset is like a torrent rolling stones; decision is like the swoop of a falcon.
To what are energy and decision likened? Energy to the bending of a crossbow; decision to the releasing of a trigger.
What may exist amid battle turmoil? Seeming disorder without real disorder, and an array without head or tail that is proof against defeat.
What do simulated disorder, fear and weakness presuppose? Perfect discipline, courage, and strength respectively.
How are order, courage and strength concealed? By subdivision, latent energy, and tactical dispositions.
How does a commander keep the enemy moving and ambush him? By deceitful appearances, sacrificing something for the enemy to snatch, and lying in wait with picked men.
What does the clever combatant rely on? Combined energy rather than too much from individuals, hence his ability to pick the right men.
To what do fighting men become like under combined energy? Rolling logs or stones, motionless on level ground but moving on a slope.
What is the energy of good fighters like? A round stone rolled down a mountain thousands of feet high.
Who is fresh and who exhausted in battle? The one first in the field and awaiting the enemy is fresh; the one second and hastening is exhausted.
What does the clever combatant impose and refuse? He imposes his will on the enemy and refuses to let the enemy's will be imposed on him.
How does a commander draw the enemy near or keep him away? By holding out advantages he draws him near; by inflicting damage he keeps him away.
How does a commander harass, starve or move the enemy? By harassing him at ease, starving him when well supplied, and forcing him to move when quietly encamped.
Where does a commander appear and march? At points the enemy must defend, and swiftly where he is not expected.
How does an army march far without distress? By marching through country where the enemy is not.
When is attack sure to succeed? When it strikes undefended places.
When is a general skillful in attack and defense? When the enemy does not know what to defend or what to attack.
What does subtlety and secrecy grant? Invisibility and inaudibility, and the enemy's fate in our hands.
When may one advance irresistibly and retire safely? By making for weak points to advance, and moving faster than the enemy to retire.
How is an enemy forced to engage behind ramparts? By attacking a place he must relieve.
How is an enemy prevented from engaging? By throwing something odd and unaccountable in his way.
How are our forces kept concentrated while the enemy's are divided? By discovering his dispositions while remaining invisible.
What is the advantage of unity against division? A whole against separate parts means we are many to the enemy's few, and an inferior force attacked by a superior one is in dire straits.
Why must the battle spot be secret? So the enemy must prepare at several points, and the numbers we face at any one point are few.
What happens when the enemy reinforces everywhere? He weakens every part: strengthening van weakens rear, rear weakens van, left weakens right, right weakens left.
Where do numerical weakness and strength come from? Weakness from preparing against possible attacks; strength from compelling the adversary to prepare against us.
What does knowing the time and place of battle allow? Concentration from the greatest distances.
What happens when neither time nor place is known? The wings cannot succor each other, nor van and rear support each other.
How is a stronger enemy prevented from fighting? By scheming to discover his plans, rousing him to reveal his activity, and forcing him to reveal his vulnerable spots.
Why compare the opposing army with your own? To know where strength is superabundant and where deficient.
What is the highest pitch of tactical dispositions? Concealment, safe from the subtlest spies and the wisest brains.
What can the multitude not comprehend? How victory is produced out of the enemy's own tactics.
What can all men see, and what can none see? All see the tactics of conquest; none see the strategy from which victory evolves.
Should tactics be repeated? No; methods must be regulated by the infinite variety of circumstances.
How are tactics like water? Water avoids high ground and flows down; in war, avoid the strong and strike the weak.
How does water shape its course, and how does the soldier win? Water follows the ground; the soldier wins in relation to the foe he faces.
What follows from water having no constant shape? Warfare has no constant conditions; he who adapts his tactics to his opponent may be called heaven-born.
Are the five elements always equally predominant? No; seasons alternate, days vary in length, and the moon waxes and wanes.
From whom does the general receive commands? From the sovereign.
What must a general do after concentrating his forces? Blend and harmonize the different elements before pitching camp.
What is the most difficult thing after harmonizing the army? Tactical maneuvering, which consists in turning the devious into the direct and misfortune into gain.
What shows knowledge of deviation? Taking a long circuitous route after enticing the enemy out of the way, and reaching the goal before him though starting after him.
When is maneuvering advantageous or dangerous? Advantageous with an army, most dangerous with an undisciplined multitude.
What are the risks of marching for advantage or detaching a flying column? You will likely be too late, or you must sacrifice baggage and stores.
What happens on a forced march of a hundred li? The leaders of all three divisions fall into enemy hands, and only one-tenth of the army arrives.
What happens on marches of fifty and thirty li? At fifty li you lose the first division's leader and half the force; at thirty li, two-thirds arrive.
What three things make an army lost? No baggage-train, no provisions, no bases of supply.
When may alliances be entered? Not until the designs of neighbors are known.
What must a general know to lead on the march? The face of the country, its mountains and forests, pitfalls and precipices, marshes and swamps.
What is needed to turn natural advantage to account? Local guides.
What practice ensures success in war? Dissimulation.
What decides concentration or division of troops? Circumstances.
How rapid and compact should an army be? As rapid as the wind and compact as the forest.
How should raiding, immobility, plans and movement be? Like fire in raiding, like a mountain in immobility, dark as night in plans, and like a thunderbolt in movement.
How should spoil and captured territory be divided? Spoil among the men, and captured territory into allotments for the soldiery.
What should precede a move? Ponder and deliberate.
Who conquers in maneuvering? He who has learnt the artifice of deviation.
Why are gongs and drums instituted? Because the spoken word does not carry far enough on the battlefield.
What do gongs, drums, banners and flags accomplish? They focus the ears and eyes of the host on one point, so the brave cannot advance alone nor the cowardly retreat alone.
How should signals be used by night and day? Signal-fires and drums by night; flags and banners by day.
What may be robbed from an army and its commander? The army of its spirit, and the commander-in-chief of his presence of mind.
When is a soldier's spirit keenest and when does it flag? Keenest in the morning, flagging by noonday, and in the evening bent only on returning to camp.
How does a clever general study moods? By avoiding an army whose spirit is keen, and attacking it when sluggish and inclined to return.
What is the art of retaining self-possession? Being disciplined and calm while awaiting disorder among the enemy.
What is the art of husbanding strength? Being near the goal while the enemy is far, waiting at ease while he toils, and being well-fed while he is famished.
What is the art of studying circumstances? Refraining from intercepting an enemy whose banners are in order, and from attacking an army in calm and confident array.
What is the axiom regarding hills? Do not advance uphill against the enemy, nor oppose him coming downhill.
What should not be pursued or attacked? An enemy simulating flight, and soldiers whose temper is keen.
What bait and what army should be avoided? The bait offered by the enemy, and an army returning home.
What is the rule for surrounding and pressing? Leave an outlet free when surrounding, and do not press a desperate foe too hard.

How should a general act in five kinds of country? Do not encamp in difficult country; join allies where roads intersect; do not linger in isolated positions; resort to stratagem when hemmed in; fight when desperate.
What five things may a general refuse? Roads not to be followed, armies not to be attacked, towns not to be besieged, positions not to be contested, and commands of the sovereign not to be obeyed.
What does understanding variation of tactics enable? Handling troops; without it, knowledge of the country's configuration cannot be turned to practical account.

How are advantage and disadvantage blended? In the wise leader's plans they are blended, so that the essential part of schemes may be accomplished, and difficulties may yield an advantage that extricates us from misfortune.
How are hostile chiefs reduced? By inflicting damage, making trouble, keeping them engaged, and holding out specious allurements.
On what should the art of war rely? On our readiness to receive the enemy and on having made our position unassailable, not on the enemy's not coming or not attacking.
What are the five dangerous faults of a general? Recklessness, cowardice, a hasty temper, a delicacy of honor sensitive to shame, and over-solicitude for his men.
What causes an army to be overthrown and its leader slain? One of the five dangerous faults of a general.
How should mountains and valleys be treated? Pass quickly over mountains and keep near valleys.
Where should an army camp in mountain warfare? In high places facing the sun, not climbing heights to fight.
What should be done after crossing a river? Get far away from it.
How should a river-crossing invader be met? Not in mid-stream; let half cross, then attack.
Where should one not meet an invader? Near a river he must cross, if anxious to fight.
How should craft be moored? Higher up than the enemy and facing the sun; do not move up-stream to meet him.
What is the sole concern in salt-marshes? To get over them quickly without delay.
How should one fight in a salt-marsh? With water and grass near, and the back to a clump of trees.
How should one camp in dry, level country? On accessible rising ground to the right and rear, with danger in front and safety behind.
What four branches of knowledge enabled the Yellow Emperor to vanquish four sovereigns? Mountain, river, salt-marsh and flat-country warfare.
What ground and places do armies prefer? High ground to low, and sunny places to dark.
How is disease avoided in camp? By care of men and camping on hard ground, so the army is free from disease and this spells victory.
How should a hill or bank be occupied? On the sunny side, with the slope on the right rear.
What should be done when a ford is swollen by heavy rains? Wait until it subsides.
How should cliffs, hollows and similar places be treated? Keep away and let the enemy approach them; face them and let the enemy have them on his rear.
Why must hilly country, ponds, reed basins and thick woods near camp be searched? For men in ambush or insidious spies are likely to be lurking there.
What does an enemy close at hand and quiet indicate? Reliance on the natural strength of his position.
What does an enemy keeping aloof and provoking battle indicate? Anxiety for the other side to advance.
What does an easily accessible enemy camp indicate? A bait.
What do movement in forest trees and screens in grass indicate? The enemy is advancing, or wishes to make us suspicious.
What do rising birds and startled beasts indicate? An ambuscade, and a sudden attack.
What do high and low dust columns indicate? Chariots advancing, and infantry approaching.
What does branching dust or moving clouds indicate? Parties collecting firewood, and an army encamping.
What do humble words with preparations, and violent language, indicate? The enemy will advance, or will retreat.
What do light chariots on the wings indicate? The enemy is forming for battle.
What do peace proposals without a sworn covenant indicate? A plot.
What does much running about with ranks forming mean? The critical moment has come.
What does some advancing and some retreating mean? A lure.
What does leaning on spears mean? Faintness from want of food.
What does water-drawers drinking first mean? The army is suffering from thirst.
What does an unsecured advantage mean? The soldiers are exhausted.
What do birds gathering and night clamor indicate? An unoccupied spot, and nervousness.
What do camp disturbance, shifted banners, and angry officers indicate? Weak authority, sedition, and weary men.
What does feeding horses grain, killing cattle, and not hanging cooking-pots mean? Determination to fight to the death.
What does whispering in knots indicate? Disaffection among the rank and file.
What do frequent rewards and punishments signify? The enemy is at the end of his resources, or in dire distress.
What do envoys with compliments indicate? A wish for a truce.
What demands great vigilance? An enemy marching up angrily and remaining facing ours without fighting or leaving.
What should be done if our troops are no more numerous? Concentrate all strength, watch closely, and obtain reinforcements; no direct attack can be made.
What happens to one who makes light of opponents? He is sure to be captured.
What happens if soldiers are punished before attachment, or not punished after? They will not be submissive, or will still be useless.
How should soldiers be treated? With humanity first, then iron discipline; this is a certain road to victory.
How is discipline affected by habitually enforced commands? Well-disciplined if enforced, bad if not.
What is the gain when a general shows confidence but insists on obedience? The gain is mutual.
What are the six kinds of terrain? Accessible, entangling, temporizing, narrow passes, precipitous heights, and distant positions.
What is accessible ground and how used? Ground freely traversed by both sides; occupy raised sunny spots first and guard supplies.
What is entangling ground and its risk? Ground abandoned but hard to re-occupy; sally if the enemy is unprepared, but disaster follows if he is prepared and you fail.
What is temporizing ground and how used? Ground where neither side gains by moving first; do not stir forth but retreat to entice the enemy, then attack part of his army.
What is the rule for narrow passes? Occupy first and garrison strongly; if the enemy forestalls you, pursue only if the pass is weakly garrisoned.
What is the rule for precipitous heights? Occupy the raised sunny spots first; if the enemy holds them, retreat and entice him away.
What is the rule at a great distance from an equal enemy? It is not easy to provoke battle, and fighting disadvantages you.
What must a general study regarding Earth? The six principles connected with Earth.
What are the six calamities of an army? Flight, insubordination, collapse, ruin, disorganization, and rout, arising from the general's faults.
What causes flight? Hurling a force against one ten times its size.
What causes insubordination and collapse? Soldiers too strong and officers too weak, or officers too strong and soldiers too weak.
What causes ruin? Angry, insubordinate higher officers giving battle from resentment before the commander can judge whether to fight.
What causes utter disorganization? A weak general, unclear orders, no fixed duties, and slovenly ranks.
What causes rout? Misjudging the enemy, engaging a larger force with an inferior one, and neglecting picked soldiers in the front rank.
What must a responsible general note? The six ways of courting defeat.

What is the soldier's best ally and the test of a great general? The country's natural formation is his ally; estimating the adversary, controlling victory, and calculating difficulties, dangers and distances test a great general.
What distinguishes the winning from the defeated general? Knowing these things and practicing them wins battles; not knowing or not practicing them means defeat.
When must a general fight against the ruler's bidding, and when not? Fight if victory is sure even against the ruler; do not fight if victory is not sure even at the ruler's bidding.
Who is the jewel of the kingdom? The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, seeking only to protect his country and serve his sovereign.
How should soldiers be regarded? As children and beloved sons, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys and stand by you unto death.
What happens with an indulgent but ineffective general? His soldiers are like spoilt children, useless for any practical purpose.
When have we gone only halfway regarding our men? Knowing our men can attack but not that the enemy is not open to attack.
When have we gone only halfway regarding the enemy? Knowing the enemy is open to attack but not that our men cannot attack.
When have we still gone only halfway regarding the ground? Knowing both enemy and our men, but not that the ground makes fighting impracticable.
What is true of the experienced soldier in motion? He is never bewildered, and never at a loss after breaking camp.
What makes victory complete? Knowing the enemy and yourself, and knowing Heaven and Earth.
What are the five constant factors in war? The Moral Law, Heaven, Earth, The Commander, and Method and discipline.
What does the Moral Law accomplish? It causes the people to be in complete accord with their ruler, following him regardless of their lives.
What does Earth comprise? Distances, danger and security, open ground and narrow passes, and the chances of life and death.
What is meant by method and discipline? Marshaling the army in subdivisions, graduations of rank, maintaining supply roads, and controlling military expenditure.
Why must the five factors be known? He who knows them wins; he who knows them not fails.
What seven considerations forecast victory or defeat? Moral law, generals' ability, Heaven and Earth, discipline, army strength, training, and constancy in reward and punishment.
How should proven counsel be treated? Retain the general who hearkens and acts on it; dismiss the one who does not.
What should a general do beyond ordinary rules? Avail himself of helpful circumstances and modify plans as circumstances favor.
What is the foundation of all warfare? Deception.
How should a commander appear to the enemy? Unable when able, inactive when using forces, far when near, and near when far.
How should a secure or superior enemy be handled? Be prepared for the secure enemy; evade the superior one.
How should a choleric opponent be handled? Irritate him, and pretend weakness so he grows arrogant.
What should be done to an enemy at ease or with united forces? Give him no rest, or separate his forces.
Where and when should a commander attack? Where unprepared and where unexpected; these devices must not be divulged.
Why do many calculations lead to victory? Many calculations before battle lead to victory, few to defeat, and none to certain loss.
What is the daily cost of a hundred thousand men? A thousand ounces of silver per day, including home and front expenditure.
What happens when victory is long in coming? Weapons dull, ardor dampens, sieges exhaust strength, and protracted campaigns strain the State.
What danger follows dulled weapons and spent treasure? Other chieftains take advantage, and no wisdom can avert the consequences.
Has any country benefited from prolonged warfare? No; none has.
Who understands the profitable way of war? Only one thoroughly acquainted with its evils.
How does a skillful soldier manage supply? No second levy, no more than twice-loaded wagons; bring material from home and forage on the enemy.
How does distant maintenance affect the people? It impoverishes them through contributions from a distance.
How does an army's proximity affect prices and the people? Prices rise, the people's substance is drained, and the peasantry suffer heavy exactions.
What is the value of foraging on the enemy? One cartload of enemy provisions equals twenty of one's own, and one picul equals twenty from one's own store.
Why must soldiers be angered and rewarded? To kill the enemy and to gain advantage from defeating him.
How should captured chariots and soldiers be treated? Reward first takers, replace flags, mingle chariots, and kindly treat and keep captured soldiers.
What should be the great object in war? Victory, not lengthy campaigns.
Who is the arbiter of the people's fate? The leader of armies, on whom peace or peril depends.
What is the best thing in the practical art of war? To take the enemy's country whole and intact; to shatter it is not so good.
What is supreme excellence in war? Breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting.
What are the grades of generalship? Balk the enemy's plans; prevent junction of his forces; attack his army in the field; and worst, besiege walled cities.
Why should siege be avoided? Mantlets, shelters, implements and mounds take six months, and an irritated general loses a third of his men.
How does a skillful leader win without fighting? He subdues troops without fighting, captures cities without siege, and overthrows kingdoms without lengthy operations.
What is the rule for unequal forces? Ten to one surround; five to one attack; twice as numerous divide; equal offer battle; slightly inferior avoid; quite unequal flee.
What is the fate of a small force in an obstinate fight? It must in the end be captured by the larger force.
What is the general's relation to the State? He is the bulwark; complete, the State is strong; defective, the State is weak.

What are the three ways a ruler brings misfortune on his army? Hobbling it by ignorant commands, causing restlessness by governing it like a kingdom, and shaking confidence by undiscriminating employment of officers.
What follows from a restless and distrustful army? Trouble from other feudal princes, anarchy in the army, and victory flung away.

What are the five essentials for victory? Knowing when to fight, handling superior and inferior forces, one spirit in the ranks, being prepared while the enemy is unprepared, and military capacity without interference.
What follows from knowing the enemy and yourself? No fear in a hundred battles; if only yourself, alternate victory and defeat; if neither, defeat in every battle.
